questions.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: The sodium–potassium pump is inhibited in a teaching model. Why might sodium–glucose uptake weaken later?

options.text: The sodium gradient gradually becomes less able to power cotransport
options.explanation: The pump maintains the gradient; its loss eventually reduces the energy available to secondary transport.

options.text: The glucose cotransporter has started hydrolysing ATP directly
options.explanation: The cotransporter does not become an ATPase when the pump is inhibited.

options.text: Every membrane channel becomes physically sealed
options.explanation: Pump inhibition does not imply physical closure of all channels.

questions.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot?

options.text: Cardiac muscle contains no calcium
options.explanation: Cardiac contraction critically depends on calcium.

options.text: The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction
options.explanation: The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.

options.text: Skeletal muscle has no electrical activity
options.explanation: Skeletal-muscle excitation normally involves action potentials.

questions.title: Autonomic signals: receptor before response
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A learner says every sympathetic postganglionic neuron releases noradrenaline. Which example corrects the claim?

options.text: All parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release dopamine
options.explanation: Parasympathetic preganglionic transmission is cholinergic, not dopaminergic.

options.text: All sympathetic ganglia release insulin
options.explanation: Insulin is not the general autonomic ganglionic transmitter.

options.text: Sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine
options.explanation: Eccrine sweat-gland innervation is the important sympathetic cholinergic exception.

questions.title: The cardiac cycle: pressure opens the valves
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL. What is stroke volume?

options.text: 70 mL
options.explanation: Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.

options.text: 170 mL
options.explanation: Adding the volumes does not measure the volume ejected.

options.text: 50 mL
options.explanation: This is the residual end-systolic volume.

questions.title: Ventilation: make each breath count
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space, which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation?

options.text: 300 mL at 20 breaths/min
options.explanation: This gives (300−150)×20 = 3 L/min.

options.text: 500 mL at 12 breaths/min
options.explanation: This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min, because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.

options.text: Both necessarily give equal alveolar ventilation
options.explanation: Equal total ventilation does not imply equal gas-exchanging ventilation.

questions.title: Water balance: distinguish ADH from aldosterone
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery?

options.text: ADH can no longer bind any receptor by definition
options.explanation: A weakened gradient does not itself establish loss of receptor binding.

options.text: Aldosterone becomes a substitute physical osmotic gradient
options.explanation: A hormone cannot substitute for the physical water-potential difference.

options.text: Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force
options.explanation: ADH makes a pathway available; the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.

questions.title: Haemostasis: build and stabilise the plug
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase?

options.text: Prothrombin to thrombin
options.explanation: Xa with Va forms prothrombinase and supports thrombin generation.

options.text: Factor X to Xa by IXa–VIIIa
options.explanation: IXa–VIIIa is intrinsic tenase, not prothrombinase.

options.text: Fibrin crosslinking by XIIIa
options.explanation: Crosslinking stabilises fibrin after its formation; it is not the prothrombinase reaction.

questions.title: Digestion: coordinate movement and secretion
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion?

options.text: Stopping all pancreatic enzyme secretion
options.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes contribute to digestion of the meal.

options.text: CCK supporting enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction
options.explanation: CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.

options.text: Converting bile into a protein-digesting enzyme
options.explanation: Bile assists lipid handling but is not a protein-digesting enzyme.

questions.title: Energy balance: connect intake, storage and use
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work?

options.text: Energy expenditure falls to exactly zero
options.explanation: Basal cellular work continues even without a meal.

options.text: The liver creates energy without using substrate
options.explanation: Hepatic metabolic pathways transform substrates and require energy; they do not create it.

options.text: Stored substrates are mobilised to support continued metabolism
options.explanation: Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.

questions.title: Endocrine axes: read the feedback loop
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Low thyroid hormone is accompanied by a TSH that is not appropriately elevated. What does this challenge in a simple model?

options.text: The assumption that the central feedback response is intact
options.explanation: An intact pituitary response to primary thyroid failure would usually raise TSH; central influences merit consideration.

options.text: The existence of any thyroid receptors
options.explanation: The pattern does not prove absence of tissue receptors.

options.text: The fact that hormones circulate in blood
options.explanation: The pattern concerns regulation, not whether hormones circulate.

questions.title: Reproductive physiology: connect the two cycles
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: After ovulation, which hormone most directly supports secretory differentiation of the endometrium?

options.text: Adrenaline acting as the only ovarian hormone
options.explanation: Adrenaline is not the principal luteal endometrial signal.

options.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum
options.explanation: Luteal progesterone supports secretory changes following estradiol-driven proliferation.

options.text: A complete absence of all ovarian hormones
options.explanation: Withdrawal of luteal hormones contributes to menstruation rather than maintenance of secretory endometrium.

questions.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined effect. What is this?

options.text: Renal filtration
options.explanation: Filtration describes a different physiological process.

options.text: Spatial summation only
options.explanation: Spatial summation combines inputs from different locations.

options.text: Temporal summation
options.explanation: Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.

questions.title: Special senses: convert a stimulus into a signal
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A hair bundle is deflected in its excitatory direction. Which initial response is expected?

options.text: Opening of mechanotransduction channels and depolarisation
options.explanation: Mechanical channel opening permits a depolarising current under the inner-ear ionic conditions.

options.text: Closure of every channel and immediate cell death
options.explanation: Normal sensory transduction does not imply injury or universal channel closure.

options.text: Conversion of the hair cell into a photoreceptor
options.explanation: The receptor retains its hair-cell identity.

questions.title: Microcirculation: return the filtered fluid
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: Two examples cause oedema: increased venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction. What differs?

options.text: Only one involves interstitial fluid
options.explanation: Both can increase interstitial fluid.

options.text: One can increase filtration; the other reduces return
options.explanation: They change different sides of the filtration–return balance.

options.text: Neither has any relationship to fluid balance
options.explanation: Both are mechanisms relevant to tissue-fluid accumulation.

questions.title: Volume I: orient the thorax around the lung root
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A diagram places the diaphragm low in the thorax. Why does this not imply thoracic motor roots?

options.text: Diaphragm contraction never uses nerves
options.explanation: The diaphragm requires motor innervation for normal contraction.

options.text: The vagus is its only somatic motor supply
options.explanation: The phrenic nerves provide the principal motor supply.

options.text: Its phrenic motor supply principally comes from C3–C5
options.explanation: Adult position and developmental history must be distinguished from segmental motor supply.

questions.title: Volume II: connect peritoneum and the portal triad
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In a conventional anterior view of the portal triad, where is the bile duct relative to the proper hepatic artery?

options.text: On the patient's right
options.explanation: The duct conventionally lies to the patient's right of the proper hepatic artery; variants exist.

options.text: Always behind the portal vein
options.explanation: The portal vein is generally the posterior triad member.

options.text: On whichever side the viewer calls right
options.explanation: Anatomical right and left refer to the patient, not the viewer.

questions.title: Volume III: follow urine through the pelvis
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which developmental pairing is correct?

options.text: Urethra forms every nephron
options.explanation: The urethra does not give rise to renal nephrons.

options.text: Ureteric bud forms the collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons
options.explanation: Reciprocal interaction between these tissues connects nephrons to the collecting system.

options.text: Renal blood vessels become all collecting ducts
options.explanation: Vascular and collecting structures are distinct developmental components.

questions.title: Volume IV: separate taste, sensation and movement
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: Which exception should accompany an anterior-versus-posterior tongue taste map?

options.text: XII supplies all taste
options.explanation: XII is principally a motor nerve for the tongue.

options.text: V3 supplies all circumvallate taste
options.explanation: General sensation through V3 does not establish this taste supply.

options.text: Circumvallate papillae receive taste fibres from IX
options.explanation: Circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the terminal sulcus but have IX taste innervation.

questions.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A diagram labels the posterior cord. Posterior relative to what?

options.text: The second part of the axillary artery
options.explanation: The artery provides the conventional landmark for brachial-plexus cord names.

options.text: Every point on the skin surface
options.explanation: Cord names are not defined relative to all skin surfaces.

options.text: The posterior tibial artery
options.explanation: This vessel is in the lower limb and does not define brachial-plexus cord position.

questions.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A section has nuclei at different heights, but every cell contacts the basal lamina. Which interpretation fits?

options.text: Stratified epithelium is certain
options.explanation: Several nuclear heights do not by themselves establish multiple cell layers.

options.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is possible
options.explanation: In pseudostratified epithelium all cells contact the basal lamina, although not all reach the surface.

options.text: It cannot be epithelium
options.explanation: This arrangement is compatible with epithelial organisation.

questions.title: PCR, qPCR and reverse transcription
questions.subject: cell-biology
questions.prompt: A PCR tube lacks one of the two primers. What is the main consequence for the intended target?

options.text: The target's sequence becomes irrelevant
options.explanation: Primer binding and template sequence determine specificity.

options.text: DNA polymerase begins every strand without a starting point
options.explanation: DNA polymerase needs an appropriate primer-template starting point.

options.text: Efficient exponential amplification of the bounded target is lost
options.explanation: The two primers define opposite ends and support amplification of both strands.

questions.title: Enzyme catalysis and inhibition
questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.prompt: In a simple reversible competitive-inhibition model, what can increasing substrate concentration do?

options.text: Reduce the inhibitor's effect on the observed rate
options.explanation: Substrate competes for binding; sufficiently high substrate can approach the same Vmax in the ideal model.

options.text: Permanently destroy the inhibitor molecule
options.explanation: Competition does not require chemical destruction of the inhibitor.

options.text: Lower the uninhibited maximum rate by definition
options.explanation: The defining ideal competitive model changes apparent Km, not Vmax.

questions.title: Complement pathways and their shared effectors
questions.subject: genetics
questions.prompt: Why can different complement activation pathways have common downstream effects?

options.text: They all begin with an identical recognition event
options.explanation: The classical, lectin and alternative pathways have distinct initiation mechanisms.

options.text: They converge on C3 activation and shared downstream components
options.explanation: Convergence explains shared effects such as C3b-mediated opsonisation despite different triggers.

options.text: They never interact with innate immunity
options.explanation: Complement is a major component of innate defence and connects with adaptive responses.
